author: liam.oconnor - Sports Editor
title: Good Wood: MLB Hitters Strike Out Less
text:
PHOENIX, Aug. 26, 2025
Hitters Are Slowly Turning the Tables on Strikeouts Major League Baseball’s hitters are showing signs of adapting to high-velocity pitching and rules changes, leading to a slight uptick in batting average.
MLB teams are averaging 8.28 hits and strikeouts per game, with batting average rising to .246. Rule changes in 2023 aimed to increase action and attendance, but strikeouts remained high. Technology like the Trajekt Arc pitching machine is helping hitters adjust to challenging pitches. Players like Luis Arráez and Nico Hoerner exemplify a new generation of contact-oriented hitters. In a tight 10th-inning battle, Arizona’s Ketel Marte battled Cincinnati’s Graham Ashcraft, fouling off blistering fastballs and sharp sliders. On the 13th pitch, marte muscled a cutter into center field for a game-winning single. While dramatic, Marte’s at-bat encapsulates a subtle but significant trend unfolding across Major League Baseball: hitters are learning to put the ball in play.
Through the first half of the season, teams are averaging 8.28 hits and 8.28 strikeouts per game. The league-wide batting average has nudged up to .246. This small gain for hitters is likely a combination of the new rules and hitters’ improved ability to adapt to pitchers’ advanced arsenals.
“Good things happen when you put it in play,” said Rangers manager Bruce Bochy, echoing a sentiment that’s easier said than done against today’s pitchers.
Diamondbacks manager Torey Lovullo sees a growing awareness among players. “It’s about being a professional hitter and putting balls in play,” he said. “still doing it with an authority, but not taking a big two-strike home run swing.” Lovullo believes a new generation of versatile hitters is emerging from the minor leagues, blending power with contact skills.
Technology Aids Adjustment The rise of advanced technology is playing a crucial role. teams now utilize pitching machines like the Trajekt Arc, which can replicate high-velocity, high-spin pitches with movement. These machines allow hitters to face virtual simulations of any pitcher, honing their timing and approach against difficult stuff.
“We’ve all got these fancy machines,” said Yankees third baseman ryan McMahon. “It kind of shows you those things and then just having an understanding of how to attack those.” he added that hitters are simply adjusting to the game’s consistently “nasty stuff.”
Contact Hitters Shine Some of the league’s most successful teams are those that excel at minimizing strikeouts. The Toronto Blue Jays (884), San Diego padres (900) and Kansas City Royals (923) are the only teams under 1,000 whiffs this season and all are in playoff contention.
San Diego’s Luis Arráez stands out as the epitome of contact hitting. With only 15 strikeouts in 514 at-bats this season, the three-time batting champion averages a strikeout every 34.27 at-bats. This remarkable consistency is a throwback to baseball’s deadball era.
While Arráez is exceptional, Lovullo is right that a new wave of young players is adept at avoiding strikeouts. Cubs second baseman Nico Hoerner, Athletics shortstop Jacob Wilson and Cleveland’s Steven Kwan rank among the league leaders in at-bats per strikeout.
Even power hitters are finding ways to improve contact. Boston’s Trevor Story, known for his strikeouts, is on pace for his lowest whiff rate since 2021. His improved contact coincides with a strong season, hitting .260 with 21 homers and 83 RBIs.
“It’s almost more of a mindset, especially with two strikes,” Story explained. He’s embraced strategies like choking up and using the entire field, particularly hitting the ball through the “four hole” into right-center, a tactic made easier by the elimination of defensive shifts.
